title: The Cross-Functional Blocker
subtitle: Five stakeholders, one blocked project, no direct authority
description: Your project is blocked. Every stakeholder owns a piece you need but none of them report to you. Five conversations stand between you and getting unblocked. Use empathy, strategy, and adaptability to clear each one.
learning_objectives: Navigate organisational blockers without positional authority
Adapt your communication style to different stakeholder types
Build reciprocal relationships that remove blockers before they form
reflection_prompt: Which stakeholder conversation was hardest to navigate, and what made it that way?
coaching_moment: Influence without authority is the highest-leverage skill in any organisation. It starts with understanding what the other person needs before you say what you need.

rounds.title: The PM Who Will Not Deprioritise
rounds.situation: Maya, the PM on the platform team, has your key dependency in her backlog at rank 14. She has no incentive to move it. Her quarterly OKR is speed, not yours.
rounds.story: The most common blocker: someone who is not against you — they just have different priorities.
rounds.coaching_moment: Never lead with 'I need you to move this up.' Lead with 'Here is how this helps you.'

choices.label: Explain how your project's success makes her platform team look good in Q3
choices.description: Align your need to her OKR before asking.
choices.consequence_hint: Maya pauses and re-reads your request. She moves it to rank 8.

choices.label: Escalate to her manager — your timeline is at risk
choices.description: Gets results fast but burns the relationship.
choices.consequence_hint: It moves to rank 5 but Maya does not speak to you warmly for the rest of the quarter.

choices.label: Offer to write the technical spec yourself so she saves time
choices.description: Removes friction by doing the work you are asking for.
choices.consequence_hint: Maya is visibly relieved. 'If you write the spec, I can have eng start next sprint.'

rounds.title: The Engineering Manager Who Says No
rounds.situation: Dev, the Eng Manager, says his team is at 110% capacity. 'I want to help but there is genuinely no slack.' He is not blocking you — he is telling the truth.
rounds.story: Sometimes blockers are real constraints, not politics. The skill is distinguishing them.
rounds.coaching_moment: When someone tells you they have no capacity, believe them first — then ask what would need to be true for capacity to exist.

choices.label: Ask: 'What would need to come off your team's plate to create space for this?'
choices.description: Turns a closed door into a problem-solving conversation.
choices.consequence_hint: Dev lists two items that your manager might be able to deprioritise. You now have a path.

choices.label: Ask if one engineer could do 20% time on your project
choices.description: A small ask is harder to refuse than a large one.
choices.consequence_hint: Dev agrees to 20% from one engineer starting next month. Slow but real.

choices.label: Accept the block and look for a workaround that removes the eng dependency
choices.description: Shows creativity and reduces the ask entirely.
choices.consequence_hint: You find a third-party library that does 80% of what you needed. Dev is impressed.

rounds.title: The Design Lead Who Has Concerns
rounds.situation: Preethi, Design Lead, wants to re-do the UX before launch. She is right that the current design is not great — but you cannot wait two sprints for a full redesign.
rounds.story: The trickiest blockers are from someone who is correct. Being right and being helpful are not always the same thing.
rounds.coaching_moment: Acknowledge that someone is right before negotiating the scope of how right they get to be right now.

choices.label: Agree the UX has issues, propose a 'good enough to ship' v1 with a committed v2 redesign in Q4
choices.description: Validates her concern, separates now from later.
choices.consequence_hint: Preethi agrees if you put the v2 commitment in writing in the project doc.

choices.label: Push back — the UX is functional enough and customers can give real feedback post-launch
choices.description: Ship-and-learn is a valid strategy but Preethi may feel overridden.
choices.consequence_hint: She agrees reluctantly. Her feedback in the retrospective later is pointed.

choices.label: Ask if she can scope the minimum design change that would make her comfortable with launch
choices.description: Delegates the scoping to her — she defines the bar.
choices.consequence_hint: Preethi scopes a 3-day fix instead of a 2-sprint redesign. You had been imagining the wrong scale.

rounds.title: The Sales Rep Who Wants a Custom Build
rounds.situation: Raj from Enterprise Sales says he has a big deal contingent on a feature that is not in your roadmap. He is not your stakeholder but his VP is your VP's peer.
rounds.story: The customer-facing pressure is real. The feature request may or may not be the right solution.
rounds.coaching_moment: Get behind the request to the actual customer problem — the feature is one solution, not the only solution.

choices.label: Ask Raj to set up a call with the customer to understand the actual need
choices.description: Go to the source before committing to a solution.
choices.consequence_hint: The customer explains a workflow problem. You realise an existing feature solves it with a config change.

choices.label: Tell Raj you can add the feature to Q4 roadmap with a written commitment
choices.description: Gives him something to take back to the customer.
choices.consequence_hint: Raj closes the deal. You have now added scope to Q4 that was not planned.

choices.label: Decline and explain how it conflicts with the platform roadmap — offer to escalate together
choices.description: Honest and transparent but requires Raj to go to his VP.
choices.consequence_hint: The VP meeting results in a more structured prioritisation process. Slower win, better system.

rounds.title: Your Manager Needs You to Pick Up a New Project
rounds.situation: Your manager Leena drops a new high-visibility project on you — exactly as your blocked project is about to launch. She frames it as an opportunity. Your team is already stretched.
rounds.story: The hardest stakeholder conversation is sometimes with your own manager.
rounds.coaching_moment: Managing up means advocating for your team's capacity, not just saying yes to every ask. The answer is never just yes or just no — it is a trade-off conversation.

choices.label: Say yes and figure it out — visibility matters right now
choices.description: Opportunistic but risks burning your team at a critical moment.
choices.consequence_hint: Launch week is chaotic. Your team delivers but two people send you 'I need a break' messages afterwards.

choices.label: Name the trade-off clearly: 'I can take this if we deprioritise X. What would you like me to drop?'
choices.description: Forces the conversation about actual capacity.
choices.consequence_hint: Leena pauses. She moves the new project to another team and notes that you managed the conversation well.

choices.label: Ask Leena to delay the new project by 3 weeks until launch is complete
choices.consequence_hint: She agrees to 2 weeks. Not perfect but workable.

glossary_terms.definition: Getting things done through persuasion, relationships, and reciprocity rather than positional power
The accumulated goodwill and trust that gives you the ability to ask for things and expect cooperation
Proactively communicating with your manager about priorities, capacity, and trade-offs rather than waiting to be directed
